speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce arising out of a press report in today's Globe and Mail. This report indicates that flax prices skidded 15 cents yesterday on the Winnipeg market. Can the minister inform the house whether the Canadian government was informed of the intention of the United States government to place surplus flax stocks on the world market and whether it is expected this action will affect the price of other grains?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: REDUCTION IN PRICE AT WINNIPEG-ACTION OF UNITED STATES GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government was not advised in advance of the action taken by the United States to cut the price of flax on the export market. The United States is not a market for Canadian flax. The entry of our flax is barred by a prohibitive duty, and that has been the situation for a number of years. Consequently it is natural that the United States would not think of Canada in connection with the marketing of flax.
Canadian flax is marketed through the Winnipeg grain exchange and I presume that

it is a reflection of the prices of flax on foreign markets that has affected the Canadian price, even though the principal market for Canadian flax is in Canada.
So far as the export price of flax affecting the price of other grains is concerned I am of the opinion the price of flax will have no relation to the prices of other grains.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE ASSISTANCE FOR HOME CONSTRUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution now before the committee seeks authorization by the house to introduce a bill to amend the Veterans' Land Act by adding to it two new parts to provide veterans with new means of assistance to build their own homes, and to settle on the land for full-time or part-time farming.
The portion of the bill to be known as part II of the Veterans' Land Act is intended further to assist veterans of world war II and the Korean operations to become home owners. It is particularly designed to assist veterans who, because of the nature and location of their employment, cannot be established conveniently on two or three acres of land as part-time farmers under the Veterans' Land Act, and whose income is not sufficient to meet payments on the cost of a home built by a regular contractor under the National Housing Act.
It has been our experience that many such veterans are capable and willing, if given technical guidance and supervision, to put their own labour into building a modern home, and thus bring its cost within their reach. The assistance we propose to provide Will consist of training courses planned to give the veterans concerned a general knowledge of housebuilding; supervision and technical guidance during construction; financing on an interest-free basis while the work is in progress; the supply of standard plans and drawings and free legal service up to and including deed and mortgage.
Under this measure there will be no conditional grant as for full-time and part-time farmers, but veterans retain their right to re-establishment credit which, if it has not been used, may form all or part of the down payment required under this proposed legislation.
It is proposed to authorize the director of the Veterans' Land Act to enter into a construction contract with an eligible veteran who, after a course of instruction or another suitable test, is considered to be competent to build his own house, and who has been approved for a loan under the National Housing Act. Before entering into such a contract, the veteran must either pay to the director not less than $800 to be used to purchase a lot, or transfer to the director title to a suitable lot worth at least that amount, or make his down payment partly in land and partly in cash. There will be no restriction as to the size of the lot provided it is suitable for a single family dwelling.
This cash or land requirement will serve, first, as a security deposit during the life of

the building contract and, second, as all or part of the veteran's down payment when the property is reconveyed to him, subject to a mortgage in favour of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or an approved lender under the National Housing Act. The cost of construction, up to a maximum of $8,000, will be financed through regular progress payments by the director from a revolving fund of $15 million. Upon completion of the house, the director will convey title to the property to the veteran and register a mortgage in favour of the lender. The proceeds of this mortgage will reimburse the revolving fund.
I know hon. members will recognize in this general outline a very close resemblance to proposals in the brief presented by the Canadian Legion to the government last November. In its brief the Legion drew attention to the success achieved under the Veterans' Land Act build-your-own-home program. Perhaps it would be helpful to refer briefly to this program, which has assisted over 9,000 veterans, most of them with only modest incomes, to achieve the stability and satisfaction of home ownership by applying their own muscle and management.
The build-your-own-home program was introduced in 1949 to overcome the ever-increasing cost of building, so far as to enable veterans to continue to become home owners under the Veterans' Land Act without committing themselves to payments which, considering their incomes, they might not be able to meet. It was realized that additional supervision would be required in connection with these contracts, and, to meet this need with the comparatively small staff of supervisors available, the Veterans' Land Act administration developed the idea of holding evening courses of instruction for prospective veteran builders. This group instruction, carried out during the winter months when construction work was at a minimum, had the effect of spreading the work of the construction supervisors more evenly over the year, and has made it possible for many veterans to undertake the construction of their own houses who, otherwise, would have been unable or have lacked confidence to do so.
As at the end of last December, about 6,650 houses had been completed by veterans acting as their own contractors, and nearly 1,800 more were under construction. Of over 1,700 new house contracts let by the director during the past year, 84 per cent were let to veterans acting as their own contractors.
Veterans Land Act
The saving to the veteran under this program is substantial. Not only does he save the contractor's profit but he generally saves substantially in labour costs by doing much of the unskilled work himself. Workmanship of the houses built to date has been at least as good as that on similar houses built by contractors. While the main credit for this must rightly go to the veterans themselves, I think the success of this program owes a great deal to the construction supervisors who have assumed the dual role of instructors and guardians of a public investment. These men will be performing a similar function under the measure proposed.
In addition to these houses built by veterans settled as part-time farmers under the act, approximately 50 have been built during recent years on city lots under a joint assistance arrangement between Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the Veterans' Land Act administration. Under this arrangement, the director conducted training schools and gave supervision and legal services during the construction period, while the financing was done by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
Included in this number are 29 houses built near the Carleton Heights Veterans' Land Act project, just outside Ottawa, by a group of junior civil servants who, for the purpose of building, formed a co-operative association. These veterans paid $750 for serviced lots, which constituted both security deposit and down payment, and constructed four-bedroom houses for $6,200, which was the amount of their mortgages. The normal cost of these units, including the land, was estimated to be $9,950, or $3,000 more than the cost to the veteran, and they are valued at the present time at over $11,000.
This plan, owing to the financial arrangement, proved rather cumbersome. The difficulties then met will, however, be overcome in the proposed legislation by the revolving fund from which the director will be able to make advances to the veteran-contractors as work progresses.
With this background of experience to draw from, we now propose legislation which will assist eligible veterans who are unable to settle as part-time farmers under the act, but who are able and willing to make substantial labour and management contributions to obtain home ownership through their own efforts.
The section of the bill which will be known as part III of the Veterans' Land Act

Veterans Land Act
will make available to full-time and parttime farming veterans and commercial fishermen veterans additional financial assistance in the form of fully repayable loans bearing interest at the rate of 5 per cent. Repayment will be amortized over a period not in excess of the remaining period of a veteran's existing contract with the director.
The purpose of making provision for these loans is twofold. Firstly, they will assist veterans who desire settlement under the Veterans' Land Act to bridge the gap between the maximum financial assistance now available and the cost of acquiring economic farm units or constructing houses. Secondly, they will provide a source of credit to veterans already settled or to be settled as fulltime farmers under the Veterans' Land Act for the purchase of additional land, erecting buildings, clearing, fencing, draining or effecting other improvements which will increase the productive value of the land and promote soil conservation.
While a source of credit for such purposes is available to the ordinary farmer under the provisions of the Canadian Farm Loan Act or the provisions of the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the fact that the veteran settled under the Veterans' Land Act does not have title to the land he farms, but is considered as a tenant at will, prevents him from obtaining any assistance available under those two acts, with the exception that he is eligible under the Farm Improvement Loans Act for loans to purchase livestock or farm implements.
The additional loans which this measure will authorize the director to make will amount to a maximum of $3,000 on behalf of full-time farmers either already settled or to be settled; and $1,400 on behalf of part-time farmers and commercial fishermen who may be settled in the future. Assistance under this part is not provided for those veterans already settled as part-time farmers or commercial fishermen, who will be able to obtain financing for extensions to their houses under part IV of the National Housing Act, which will make provision for home improvements and home extension loans when it is proclaimed.
I have indicated, Mr. Chairman, the maximum amount of loan that the director will be authorized to make. To qualify for such a loan the veteran will be required to contribute an amount equal to one-half of the loan. That is, if the cost of purchasing additional loans or effecting improvements totals $4,500, then the veteran will contribute $1,500 to be used in conjunction with the loan to be made by the director amounting to $3,000.

However, a cash contribution by the veteran may not be required in all instances. If a veteran had an equity in a property at the time he was settled under the Veterans' Land Act, or if, since the date of his settlement, he has increased the value of the property by way of improvements at no cost to the director, then the amount of such equity or increase in value will be considered as all or part of the veteran's cash contribution.
With the additional financial assistance which this measure will provide, it will be possible for a veteran already settled, or seeking settlement as a full-time farmer, to obtain total financial assistance amounting to $9,000, so that the maximum funds available for expenditure on his behalf, including his contribution, will be $10,500.
In so far as the new part-time farmer or commercial fisherman is concerned, the maximum funds available for expenditure on his behalf, including his contribution, would be $8,100.
It is believed that the provisions of this bill, in conjunction with the build-your-own-home program and the assistance and service provided by the administration's well-trained and experienced staff of supervisors, will have the effect of bringing the over-all financial assistance available under the Veterans' Land Act into line with the price structure of today without, at the same time, involving any veteran in commitments he might not be able to meet.
It is proposed, Mr. Chairman, that when this bill receives second reading it will be referred to the special committee dealing with veterans legislation where, of course, there will be ample opportunity for full explanations by the responsible officials of the department.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE ASSISTANCE FOR HOME CONSTRUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I followed the minister as best I could during his rather technical and involved statement which was rather difficult to grasp. However, as there will be a bill following this and the matter will be discussed in the veterans affairs committee, we will then have a better opportunity of understanding it and making whatever comments may be necessary.
I might say at the outset, Mr. Chairman, that I am in hearty agreement with the principle, as I understood it, which was outlined by the minister. The only criticism I would make is that it is rather late in coming. I think this is a matter which could have been dealt with some time ago and, as the minister himself pointed out, this principle has been suggested by the opposition on different occasions, and advanced in particular by the Canadian Legion.

There has been great concern during the last five or six years over the serious housing shortage as far as veterans and others are concerned, I think particularly in the case of veterans, because they have been to my mind the greatest sufferers in terms of this housing shortage. The Legion has made a very serious study of this matter since 1948 when they made recommendations to the government on how they felt the housing situation could be improved. They realized, as we all do, that the present housing situation does not meet the need so far as the veterans are concerned, and also that the Veterans' Land Act did not meet the requirements of the Legion.
There has been particular criticism of the fact that under the Veterans' Land Act veterans could not obtain lots and build in towns and cities. I understand from the minister's statement today that this is to be corrected. Many of our veterans build on two and three acre lots and they find that trying to farm, and also carry on other work, is quite impractical. It was more of a rural than an urban scheme and, in order to meet the requirements, this small city lot proposal was introduced which I think will meet the demand.
This criticism, of course, was advanced by veterans who were commuters and therefore did not have time to carry on extensive gardening or farming on their three-acre lot, and many found in addition that the high cost of machinery prevented them from carrying out the work they had intended. They now find that many of these lots are heavily under weeds and that the situation is not at all satisfactory.
The resolution before us suggests that there will be financial and technical assistance, and the minister has mentioned the fact that this assistance will be in the form of a revolving fund which will not place a heavy burden on the taxpayers of this country, since it will be in the form of a loan to veterans which they will be able to pay back under the provisions outlined by the minister. I believe this is a very sound idea, and we can take from what the minister said this afternoon that it is the intention of the government to implement the suggestion in the Legion's brief of November 1953 which called for a substantial extension of the Veterans' Land Act.
The build-your-own-home idea, about which we have heard a great deal from veterans in the past, received the blessing of the then minister of veterans affairs, the present Minister of Labour, in 1948, and it has proved very successful. It is based on
Veterans Land Act
the idea of self-help as well as mutual assistance. I did not understand the minister to say whether a veteran building on his own could receive assistance from his fellow veterans, and I do not know whether that is the intention of the government. Perhaps he could tell us now. Is that the intention?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE ASSISTANCE FOR HOME CONSTRUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE ASSISTANCE FOR HOME CONSTRUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
As I say, it is a matter of mutual help as well as self-help. The idea of providing schools of instruction and providing that the veteran himself can attend school and learn something about construction and building, where other veterans also attend those schools and where one veteran will help another, is a good one. It certainly means that by their united efforts they will be able to build their houses much more cheaply than otherwise.
It is a fact also that the veteran will not require to have as much income. When the National Housing Act was under discussion in the house some time ago I think it was stated that a home builder must have an income of at least $3,800 in order to construct his home under the National Housing Act. This afternoon the minister told us that a much smaller salary will be all that is necessary for a veteran to have in order to take advantage of this new bill that is proposed.
The minister also told us that some 6,500 houses had already been built under the build-your-own-home scheme, and that of that number some 800 I think were under construction this year. I understand that in the building of these homes, which cost in the vicinity of $6,000, by this self-help and mutual help the veteran has been able to save anywhere from $2,000 to $4,000 per house. That is indeed a great saving and it is of great benefit to the veteran. The minister has also pointed out that under the present Veterans' Land Act scheme-which I think is operating under order in council- for these build-your-own-homes, schools have been set up and a pattern has already been established which will be of great benefit when this act comes into force.
The Legion makes a number of recommendations which I understand from the minister are being incorporated in the act. As a matter of fact, I think we can thank the Legion as well as the government for this proposed act. From what the minister told us this afternoon I am satisfied that this idea originated back in 1948 under Colonel Price, who was then president of the Canadian Legion. It was recommended by the Legion

Veterans Land Act

I should just like to put on the record, it I may, Mr. Chairman, the recommendations of the Canadian Legion in their brief presented to the Prime Minister and his cabinet on November 10, 1953. To me the brief indicates what a thorough study has been made of this matter by the Canadian Legion; and what influence this study and these recommendations have had upon the government is indicated by the minister's speech this afternoon. In the brief presented on November 10, 1953, the Legion made these recommendations:
We recommend that the facilities of the V.L.A. administration be made available to carry out a "Build Your Own Home" program for veterans on city size lots on the following terms:
(1)	A veteran to be eligible must have service which would qualify him for settlement under V.L.A.
(2)	The veteran must have title to a suitable lot supplied with water, or sufficient funds to purchase such a lot; the lot to be turned over to the director as security for original advances and should the appraised value of the lot be less than $800, the veteran to deposit the difference with the director.
(3)	A veteran, to qualify, must have a good employment record over a period of at least 4 years, must have taken a course in house construction using the V.L.A. syllabus and standards, and be approved as qualified to take a contract to build his home.
(4)	The veteran must be able to furnish a bond of indemnification to the director, payable in case of loss or misuse of material supplied and paid for by the director on delivery and before it is incorporated in the house.
(5)	The veteran's plan must be approved as being practical and giving good value, and the veteran must agree to build in accordance with V.L.A. standards and to accept supervision to assure the following of these standards.
(6)	The veteran to be given a contract to build at a price not to exceed 80 per cent of the value of the lot and completed house.
(7)	The director to undertake to advance money when work is completed by subcontractor or material is supplied to site, up to a total of, but not exceeding 75 per cent, of the appraised value of.the structure as it stands, and the material on the site at the time such payment is made.
(8)	Payments to be authorized by the V.L.A. construction supervisor on bills approved by the veteran-contractor direct to subcontractor or supplier of material.
(9)	The lot and completed house to be sold to the veteran at the contract price, the director taking back a mortgage on terms and at interest rate acceptable to C.M.H.C. who may purchase the mortgage, making necessary the appropriation by parliament to V.L.A. of only a circulating fund for the purpose of financing veterans' homes during the period of construction.
As we listened to the minister this afternoon we realized how closely the government is following the recommendations of the Legion in this respect. I think they are to be commended for that procedure. When this act is amended and when these ideas come

into force and are acted upon, I am satisfied that it will be of great benefit to the veteran and will assist very greatly in the building of veterans homes.
As I said at the outset, Mr. Chairman, this is a rather complicated matter and one which it is difficult to understand just by hearing a statement from the minister. We shall have ample time to study it when the bill comes down. We shall have further time to study it when the bill is before the veterans affairs committee. We can discuss it later on with more knowledge of it.

subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING

speakeroldname: Hon. Lionel Chevrier (Minister of Transport) moved
subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 442, an act respecting the construction of lines of railway by Canadian National Railway Company from St. Felicien to Chibou-gamau and from Chibougamau to Beattyville,

Canadian National Railways all in the province of Quebec, and from Hills-port on the main line of the Canadian National Railways to Manitouwadge lake, both in the province of Ontario.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the object of this bill is to construct two lines of railway, one in the province of Ontario from Hillsport, which is on the main line of the Canadian National Railways, to lake Manitouwadge, a distance of twenty-seven miles, at a cost of $3,750,000. The Ontario line will have an average cost per mile of $138,888. Statistics which have been furnished to the government by the Canadian National Railways indicate that this will be a profitable operation. In fact the statistics, which I take it will be established in the committee, prove that the potential traffic in the lake Manitouwadge area is as follows: inbound traffic, 60,000 tons per year, outbound traffic, 665,000 tons per year.
The earning power therefore of this line will be about $1,900,000 from the inbound traffic and about $4,100,000 from the outbound traffic, a total of $6 million. It follows from this that with a potential earning of $6 million per year the balance sheet of the Canadian National Railways will be bettered to that extent. There is included in the statistics which have been furnished by the Canadian National Railways a minimum traffic figure and that minimum is 700 tons of ore per day. Even with that volume, the position of this line has been established as a profitable one.
The other line from St. Felicien to Beatty-ville is 294 miles in length and will cost $35 million, that is, from Beattyville to Cache lake, $17 million; and $17 million for the easterly portion of the line, that is from Cache lake to St. Felicien; and $1 million from the junction of the two lines at Cache lake to Chibougamau itself. The cost per mile of the east end of the line, that is from St. Felicien to Chibougamau, is $122,308, while the cost per mile of the westerly end, that is from Chibougamau to Beattyville, is $114,093.
In 1953 the Canadian National Railways made a preliminary survey of this whole area and found, as they knew before from aerial photographs, that the whole area is heavily timbered. The forest resources of that section between Beattyville and Chibougamau are estimated at 30 million cords of pulpwood per year. The area from St. Felicien to Chibougamau is also heavily timbered, and there the estimate is 15-7 million cords of pulpwood per year. There is, therefore, almost twice as much timber and pulpwood on the westerly section of line as on the easterly section.


There is another point which is of importance in that regard, and it is this. On the westerly end of the line the rivers flow into Hudson bay, and therefore in the development of this area the railway line will be used to move timber from the Chibougamau into other parts of the province of Quebec. This condition does not exist in the eastern section. In the eastern section the rivers flow into Lake St. John, and therefore this pulpwood and timber will normally flow down the rivers rather than use the railways. It has been possible, for that reason, for the Canadian National Railways to obtain guarantees from certain timber companies on the western end of the line which they could not obtain on the eastern end.
In the area between Beattyville and Chibougamau there is considerable mining development, and it has been staked out by a number of companies. As it is now, the Dome Mines Company has staked a number of claims. The Opemiska and the Campbell Chibougamau Mines Limited are among those companies that have staked out claims, and both have excellent promise of development. The bulk of the prospective traffic would consist of mining concentrates moving to the Noranda smelter. As it is now the Canadian National holds guarantees from Opemiska Copper Mines Limited and Campbell Chibougamau Mines Limited, under which the two companies guarantee the shipment of a daily average of 325 tons of ore concentrates over the line from Chibougamau to Beattyville in a period of six years. It is not possible to obtain similar guarantees on the eastern end of the line.

speechtext:

I was dealing with the guarantees, and I had said that guarantees had been given by the two copper mines that I mentioned. There was also a guarantee from the Howard Smith company, in which they undertake to move
30,000	cords of pulpwood per year for a period of six years. I was going on to say that it was because of these guarantees the Canadian National Railways came to the decision that they should build from the west end, namely from Beattyville to Chibougamau first. However, as I pointed out earlier, the Lake St. John area has a great future from the point of view of economic development. There is no doubt that, because of the tremendous amount of water power that is available in that area, and because of the proximity of an important seaport, it will be possible to continue the line in that area which will open up new territory.
The directors of the Canadian National Railways, after having carefully considered, over a period of time, the economics of the whole line have come to the conclusion that the line should be built as a whole in the general interests of Canada, and we in the government conceive it as one line. We are asking for authority to construct it as a whole. We will start from the west end. There is sufficient assurance of traffic from the west end. Construction from this end can be commenced without a subsidy or special arrangement, and without awaiting further development. With regard to the eastern portion it will be necessary to see what assurances of economic developments exist, and it will be necessary also to ascertain whether or not some sort of subsidy arrangement such as was made in the case of the P.G.E. and the Ontario Northland, in contemplation of northern development, should be made.
However, both the railway and the government feel there is sufficient assurance of future development to ask parliament now to authorize this line, but there is not sufficient assurance on which to base any definite arrangement to finance the whole of the line at this time. It was for that reason I made the statement at the resolution stage of the bill that we would proceed in the manner in which we are. It does not follow from that decision that it will not be possible to
Canadian National Railways begin construction at the eastern end soon, but thus far there has been no tangible evidence of any guarantee of traffic from the eastern end of the line. Until there is I do not think this house would want the government to proceed with a venture in which the Canadian National Railways might involve itself in a serious financial position. I think we are safe in proceeding in the way in which we are. We are taking no chances. There are guarantees on the western portion of the line, in the same manner as there were guarantees on the Barraute-Kiask Palls line. There is no difference at all in the method of procedure here by the Canadian National Railways, and what was done in respect of the earlier line.

speechtext: Would the minister permit a question? Could the minister tell us what happened in connection with the Barraute guarantee? I would be interested in the figures, in a general way, if he has them.

subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext:
Yes. I think I can safely say this, that the Barraute to Kiask Falls line has worked out far better than had been expected. The house will recall that when the line was built I made certain statements of the estimated profits that would accrue to the Canadian National Railways if that line were built, and I also gave the house the assurance that the Canadian National Railways had obtained guarantees from Canada Pulp and Paper or Howard Smith Paper Mills, Limited, I am not sure which. Those guarantees were given for a period of five or six years. The guarantees have been exceeded; and the position of the Canadian National Railways as a result of the construction of that line has been bettered.
As a matter of fact I have the record here on that point, and perhaps I should give it to the house. At the time the construction of the Barraute-Kiask Falls line was authorized the Canadian National Railways estimated the operating result for the first six years would be as follows: Total gross revenue of the C.N.R., $3,007,000; total expenses, $2,316,000; net system revenue, $691,000 before interest and $97,000 net profit.
The pulpwood traffic guarantee for those years obtained from Canada Pulp and Paper was a minimum guarantee for the first year of 40,000 cords, and a minimum guarantee for the succeeding five years of 45,000 cords, with a total guarantee for the period of six years of 330,000 cords.
Here is what happened: For the first year- that is 1949-the shipments ran to 40,114 cords; in 1950, it was 58,474; in 1951 it was 129,536; in 1952 it was 97,744 and in 1953

Canadian National Railways it was 123,232, for a five-year period total of 449,100 cords. This means that in the first five years of operation pulpwood shipments exceeded the guarantee for the first six years by 119,100 cords. So that the estimate of the Canadian National Railways in that case has proved to be pretty sound.
When the hon. member interrupted I believe I was about to make the point that the Canadian National Railways have given careful consideration to the economics of the situation. They believe that the economics prove that this line should be built. They would like to begin at the west end, and they believe that by the time they get to Chibou-gamau they will have obtained traffic guarantees. If they have not succeeded in so doing, I hope that industrial development in that area will be such that they can continue completion of the line.
As I said earlier, at the resolution stage, it is my intention when this bill has received second reading to refer it to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines for consideration.

The first point is this, that the resolution we passed on May 11 was one to authorize expenditure of $38,750,000. subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext:
In section 4 of the bill. And as I have been asked the question, Mr. Speaker, perhaps I might be permitted to read that section. It says:
Subject to the provisions of this act and the approval of the governor in council, the company may, in respect of the cost of the construction and completion of the railway lines, or to provide amounts required for the repayment of loans made under section 5, issue notes, obligations, bonds, debentures or other securities (in this act called "securities"), not exceeding in the aggregate, exclusive of any securities issued to secure loans made under section 5, the sum necessary to provide the company with the net amount of forty-four million five hundred and sixty-two thousand five hundred dollars, bearing such rates of interest and subject to such other terms and conditions as the governor in council may approve.
I believe that under the rules of the house the amount contained in the bill should be the amount authorized by the resolution. I draw


this to the minister's attention for an explanation. In the figures he gave us today respecting the cost of this line he repeated the amounts contained in the schedule which, of course, add up to $38,750,000. So there is no explanation in the schedule as to how the larger amount is reached.
Then the second point on which I should like to have further explanation is the statement that one part of the line is going to be built first, and then the other part is to be built later, or that it may be built later. Usually when these bills are brought in making provision for the construction of a railway line they authorize such construction from one point to another, and set out a time within which the line is to be built.
I have before me the bill which authorized the extension from Terrace to Kitimat, in British Columbia, as it is set out in chapter 20 of the statutes of 1952. The procedure I have outlined is, I suggest, the normal one- to provide for the building of a line from point A to point B within a certain period of time.
In the bill we are asked to pass today I find a change in this procedure. According to this bill the line may be built in whole or in part at the discretion of the governor in council, and it need not be built until 1964. Well, that is ten years from now. I would point out that in the Terrace-Kitimat bill the line was to be built before November 1, 1954. I think there was a similar provision in the Lynn Lake bill-that is, that the line was to be built right away.
In the bill before us however we find that for some reason or other there is a provision permitting a delay of ten years. The minister has said the company will begin to build the railway from the west end, that is from Beattyville to Chibougamau, and that they have guarantees of a certain amount of freight for that portion of the line. But when it comes to the line from Chibougamau to St. Felicien he is not so clear. He says it will be necessary to see what assurance of economic development exists in the Lake St. John area, to be traversed by this eastern portion of the line. I think he said something to the effect that there was not sufficient assurance to finance the whole of the line at this time. Also he used words to this effect, that there is no tangible evidence of any guarantee of traffic.
He was very indefinite about the building of this other half of the line. I raised this question when the resolution was under debate because it seemed strange to me that the minister would come into the house and ask authority to build a line and not be prepared to build from both ends at once. Instead of that he is planning obviously to

build one, and then he can see whether or not the other is to be built, and yet he has authority to go ahead if it is decided at that time to go ahead.

To me, as someone coming from a long distance away from where this line is to be built, it would seem that the best way to build up industries in there would be to build this line now and not wait for ten years to build it. It is asking quite a lot to expect others to build up industries when they are not getting a line. I cannot quite see the minister's reasoning in that regard.
I believe that the Lake St. John and Chicoutimi and Saguenay area is being seriously prejudiced by this policy of the government. Mr. Speaker, the public bodies and the people of the Lake St. John-Saguenay district are satisfied that potential traffic in the immediate future is more than sufficient to convince the authorities of the Canadian National that the eastern and western sections of the line should be built at the same time. On their behalf I beg the government to undertake immediately the building of the St. Felicien-Chibougamau section.
The main factor that was taken into consideration by the authorities of the Canadian National Railways in deciding to build the eastern section was the guarantee of an average traffic of some 325 tons of ore per day, and the promise by the Howard Smith Paper company to ship some 30,000 cords of pulpwood or approximately 175,000 tons per year.

Mr. Speaker, the bill now before us will have far-reaching consequences for the whole Saguenay kingdom, and most particularly for the constituency which I have the honour of representing in this house, provided that a clause be inserted stipulating that the two sections of the trunk line shall be undertaken and completed at the same time.
If the Chibougamau-Beattyville section is built, while the Chibougamau-St. Felicien section is deferred, we will have a trunk line

whicn was started the wrong way and which will benefit the Toronto financiers before the people of Quebec.
Some say that the name Chibougamau comes from an Indian word meaning "land of hope" or "promised land". To the prospectors, mining engineers and settlers who have visited this vast district, Chibougamau is undoubtedly a very promising land, because of the immense wealth of its subsoil. That part of the province will eventually become highly developed and there is no doubt that, one day, it will become one of the great mining districts of this country, taking its place alongside such districts as those of Porcupine, Kirkland Lake, Sudbury, Flin Flon, Noranda and Trail, even promising to surpass some of these.
It is also a new paradise for hunters and fishermen. There are wonderful lakes there, and rivers overflowing with fine trout. These lakes, some of which are quite large, are surrounded by remarkable mountains and valleys with the finest forest cover. It is an attractive district of one thousand square miles, approximately, which pleases and enthralls at first sight.
Its underground wealth was probably first recognized, back in 1906, by one Joseph Obalski, an outstanding mining engineer and geologist attached to the Quebec department of mines, who travelled throughout it and studied it at that time. It was also surveyed by Peter McKenzie, a very experienced prospector, as well as by John E. Hardman, first president of the Canadian Mining Institute.
As long as there was no easy access to that district, its exploration remained extremely costly and its development practically impossible. To reach Chibougamau one had to travel 200 miles by canoe, with about fifty portages, in summer, and a long drive by dog-sled in the cold season. In spite of this, Peter McKenzie and his son kept on with their work of exploration in that area for quite a long time.
A few years ago the building of a carriage road into that distant territory was begun, but construction was interrupted at the beginning of the last world war. Thanks to the Hon. Antonio Talbot, minister of highways of the province of Quebec, and to the Union Nationale government, work on this road was resumed in 1945, and it is possible today to drive comfortably to the very heart of that rich mining district. One of the many advantages of that road, apart from encouraging the establishment of rural parishes and opening up of new territories, is
Canadian National Railways that anyone going in for mining may transport the heavy material needed for that purpose.
That region, as well as the whole Abitibi district with Chicoutimi and the Saguenay river as its natural outlet, is, as the hon.' Minister of Transport just said, one of the gems of the kingdom of the Saguenay.

Speaking in Arvida on August 19, 1952, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said:
The kingdom oi the Saguenay and the province of Alberta are the two regions of Canada which are the most promising and assured of an extraordinary industrial development.
By plane, the Saguenay district is 50 minutes from Quebec city, two hours and 15 minutes from Montreal and four hours from New York. By car, it is three hours from Quebec city on a first-class three-lane hard surface highway. By train, the district is an overnight trip from Montreal or Quebec. The district is served by Canadian National Railways. By boat the district is in touch with the entire world. The navigation season is from April 1 to December 1. The district has two modern harbours, Chicoutimi and Port Alfred located some 15 miles east of Chicoutimi on Ha! Ha! bay.
The harbour of Chicoutimi is situated on the Saguenay river about 75 miles from its mouth. The Saguenay flows into the St. Lawrence river at a point 120 miles below Quebec. The facilities operated by the national harbours board include 2,500 linear feet of wharf accommodating ships of 26 feet draft and about 8,500 feet of standard gauge railway tracks connecting with the Canadian National Railways. In terms of tonnage handled, Port Alfred is the third largest ocean port in Canada, next to Montreal and Vancouver. It is 2,795 miles from Liverpool, England, and 810 miles from Halifax, Nova Scotia.
(Translation):
Until now the natural resources of the Abitibi region have, in the main, contributed to the wealth of citizens from other provinces. That new branch line must not help in an even greater measure to drain those vast resources which belong first of all to the citizens of the province of Quebec.
It is therefore necessary to build section A at the same time as section B, if not before.
One must first turn to the nearest seaport, that is to Chicoutimi.
The Chibougamau region is geographically related to Chicoutimi and to ignore it would be to work against the natural characteristics of the district and against present-and especially future-economic conditions.

The water power which it will be possible to harness on various rivers-the Ashuap-muchuan, Mistassini, Peribonka, and Saguenay rivers for instance-represents millions of horsepower which will be added to the existing capacity, and that fact is a powerful and fundamental argument in favour of the immediate construction of the St. Felicien branch line. The people of the Saguenay district have been clamouring for that railroad for the past forty years.
If the government truly wishes to provide our district and our province with a means of transportation that will ensure the development of that territory, it should take the whole problem into consideration right now and bring about a solution that will not only take care of present conditions but also of the future expansion and of the permanent interests of Chibougamau.
The authorities of the Canadian National should envision more than the matter of immediate profits. Since water shipping is less costly, it is usually preferred when available.
The distance between Chibougamau and Chicoutimi by rail is 220 miles, of which 139 miles remain to be built. The distance between Chibougamau-Barraute and Mont Laurier-Montreal is 515 miles of which 350 remain to be built, while the line between Chibougamau-Barraute-Noranda-North Bay and Toronto is 750 miles, of which only 165 miles remain to to be built.

And even in winter, the distance between Chibougamau and Montreal and Quebec being shorter by way of Chicoutimi, transportation costs to or from Chibougamau would again be greatly reduced. The importance of such a position from a commercial point of view is evident.
Chicoutimi is one of the national harbours which have been entrusted to a federal agency.
It would be of advantage to make use of its facilities, provided they are improved, to ship ore from the north of the province and handle incoming traffic.
This port, which is showing today a deficit, would probably become a paying undertaking of national importance.
The workmen of my constituency, who are second to none in Canada, would also benefit from it, and an element of stability would be added to the prosperity now enjoyed by 100,000 good Canadians. This part of the problem deserves attention. I believe that
[Mr. Gagnon.)

seasonal unemployment such as is experienced yearly in our cities and towns would eventually disappear, or at least would seriously diminish, were new industries born of the economic development of Chibougamau to be set up next to those already in existence.
Our region ranks first when it comes to the pulp and paper industry which provides employment for 5,000 workers, producing more than 2,200 tons of paper daily and paying out annual wages in excess of $10 million. It also ranks first with regard to production of power, and also as far as aluminum production is concerned, that industry providing work for 6,500 people whose annual income is over $11 million. It also ranks first with regard to lumbering, an industry which provides the inhabitants of the Saguenay district each year with over $11 million in wages.
It ranks first in Canada for rural trade, both wholesale and retail. Furthermore, it has the highest birth rate in North America; its population, in 1851, was 6,000 while its present population is 175,000, hence a natural increase of 34-4 per 1,000 inhabitants.
In his speech of May 11 last, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) stated that the government was not convinced of the necessity to provide subsidies for that line, but he admitted, on the other hand, that subsidies had been granted in 1949 for the extension of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway line from Quesnel to Prince George. On that occasion, that is on November 25, 1949, as shown on page 2243 of Hansard, volume III, second session, the minister stated:
The bill is a simple one. There is a precedent, not recent but many years ago, and in granting a subsidy to the P.G.E., the bill takes the form of other acts by which subsidies have been granted.
That simple bill provided for a subsidy of $15,000 per mile, on a distance of 83 miles, with an approximate cost of $8,000,000, or an average of $96,700 per mile. The total subsidy amounted to $1,240,500.
The minister added, and I quote from page 1448, volume II of Hansard for the second session of 1949:
There is a precedent for this practice. In 1913, the government proceeded in the same manner for the Ontario Northland Railway, and paid a subsidy of $6,400 per mile.
The construction of the extension will provide traffic for the railway and assist in developing the natural resources in the area consisting of large tracts of timber suitable for lumber, newsprint, pulpwood and plywood, mining possibilities, sec-

tions of agricultural and grazing lands, hydroelectric power potentialities, and sport and recreational attractions.
Mr. Speaker, we find all those resources and potentialities in the district lying between St. Felicien and Chibougamau. It it was deemed advisable to grant a subsidy to British Columbia for the development of those resources, why would the same practice not apply to Quebec? If a smelter and a refinery were not necessary in British Columbia to warrant a grant, why should they be indispensable in the province of Quebec? Why not follow the precedents in the present case and give to the bill before us "the same form as other bills of that kind", as the minister said?
What are the reasons, the motive compelling this government to discriminate as between one district and another? I, for one, cannot see any serious reason.
I know for sure that the Minister of Transport is well disposed towards us and that he is trying to treat everybody with fairness. I am also aware that the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), as member for Quebec East and head of the state, has a twofold interest in that project. They alone have the power to order the authorities of the Canadian National Railways to accede to the desire and wishes of the people of the whole province of Quebec and, in particular, of the kingdom of the Saguenay. I would therefore ask them to use their influence and to take this matter up with the proper authorities before it is too late.
In making this request, Mr. Speaker, I am expressing the wishes of everybody in my constituency, of the civil authorities, chambers of commerce or labour unions. I have received letters and telegrams asking me to take this matter up with the government. Among the telegrams which I have received I would like to mention those from the chambers of commerce of Ha! Ha! Bay and Chicoutimi, from the city councils of Chicoutimi, Bagotville and Port Alfred, from the county council of Chicoutimi, from the junior board of trade of the kingdom of the Saguenay, the Chicoutimi junior board of trade and the general council of the national syndicates. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the people of my constituency are unanimous in requesting that the government grant us this railway line which we are entitled to.
We have never been pampered in the past and the minister knows it. The province of Quebec has never had as much trackage as 83276-309

It would not be exaggerated to ask the minister, today, to see that justice is done to us. I rely on his generosity to see that this is done.

Mr. Speaker, I have only a few words to say on the bill now/ before the house. Personally, I suggest this bill might very well have been entitled simply "An act respecting the construction of a railway line by the Canadian National Railways from Chibougamau to Beattyville".
I know that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) has told us that the government intends to build eventually the second part of this railway line which, according to the minister, is to run from Beattyville to St. Felicien, via Chibougamau. Unfortunately, this bill, as it now reads, will bury in oblivion the line from St. Felicien to Chibougamau. The minister has made this very clear this afternoon-and we must admit that he spoke very plainly-when he put forward some very good reasons, of course, for constructing a line from Beattyville to Chibougamau. He was very frank also when he told us that they would build the western end first and that if, after further consideration, they found that the development of the other area could justify the building of the eastern end of the line, well, perhaps the government or the Canadian National Railways would decide to build the section from Chibougamau to St. Felicien.
My argument is, therefore, simply that the present bill only covers the western section of the railroad, from Beattyville to Chibougamau. I may be wrong, but I think that the intention has been either to deceive the

people of Lake St. John or have them believe that the government, while not pretending to have forgotten them, was postponing indefinitely the carrying out of this project, as may easily be seen by reading section 1 of the bill, which says:
That the governor In council may provide for the construction prior to the 31st day of December 1964, or such later date as the governor in council may fix.
Well, Mr. Speaker, according to the information furnished us by the hon. minister this afternoon, no railroad can be constructed if there is no guaranteed revenue to justify such an expense.
It is clear that in ten years from now, if the construction of the eastern end of the line is not undertaken immediately, the chambers of commerce, the economic council of the Lake St. John district and other civic organizations will come back to Ottawa to ask once more for the construction of a railway line between St. Felicien and Chibou-gamau. It is agreed and indeed the history of Canada proves that the construction of a railway line ensures the opening up of a district, attracts business and industry and brings about a development which otherwise would not be possible.
When the people of the St. Felicien or of the Lake St. John district come here and ask for the construction of the east end of the line, they will simply be told:	"Well, we already
have a railway line in the Chibougamau district. If you can provide us with the economic means to support this railway, well, we shall see what can be done". When they return home, these people will be in the same position as they are now, for one must not forget that two or three years ago, as I can remember, from 80 to 100 trucks loaded with all kinds of supplies went from St. Felicien to Chibougamau via the road constructed by the provincial government; the suppliers and small manufacturers of the Lake St. John district made a good deal of money and their situation improved every year.
There is no doubt that if a railroad is built between Chibougamau and Beattyville, with the line going from there to Noranda and Ontario, all the mines in Chibougamau will soon get their supplies from that part of Quebec and Ontario, before they can get their supplies from St. Felicien and the rest of Lake St. John district.
I believe that the government is wrong in turning away from the seaport of Chicoutimi. I do not think a more ludicrous instance can 83276-309i
Canadian National Railways be found than that of a government building a very costly railroad to bring mineral ore which lies scarcely 220 miles away from one of the best seaports of the country to blast furnaces established many hundred miles away.
I believe that the population of the Lake St. John region, of Chicoutimi and of the wonderful Saguenay district is entitled to demand from the government an undertaking that if the building of a railroad from Beattyville to St. Felicien via Chibougamau is undertaken, the whole line will be built and that if only part of it is to be built, the eastern branch will be built first for the reasons I have just put forward.

ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to add a few remarks to what has been said here in connection with the building of the railroad between Chibou-gamau and St. Felicien.
When it was announced that the Chibou-gamau-St. Felicien railroad would be built, the whole Saguenay district rejoiced and saw the crowning moment of forty years of efforts and representations. The people felt that at last recognition was being given to an undeniable fact, namely, that the Saguenay


district is a natural outlet for the iron ore development of Chibougamau and of great importance to its progress.
On behalf of all important organizations of the Saguenay district the council for economic planning went many times to Ottawa and in a detailed brief stated the case for the building of the branch line between Chibougamau and the Lake St. John district and insisted on its urgency. It is probably following such evident representations, which, by the way, have made known the development and great promises of the Saguenay district, that the district has been, in principle, included in the bill.
The city of Quebec itself, seeing in the outlet of Chibougamau and the Saguenay the best way to ensure for Quebec the refining of its ores, was unanimous in supporting our requests. Apparently, the government had also understood those obvious reasons, and no doubt, it was believed, the action of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) who had himself realized the immediate interest for Quebec in seeing that the project should be maintained and that the bill be now introduced.
Now, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) announces that the Abitibi-Chibou-gamau section will be built first, and moreover that this section will not be built immediately after the other, but only when the industrial development of Saguenay would urgently call for its construction.
That was, Mr. Speaker, a destruction of the magnificent impact this statement of policy had had. This is giving it, as the member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) said so well, a first-class funeral, as far as the portion which was supposed to extend into Saguenay is concerned. Thus we will be lagging behind the other area equally concerned in this matter. That statement of the hon. minister left the citizens of my county dumbfounded, especially those who live in that part of the Saguenay region which is affected. The government took a step that was called for when it announced the construction of the Chibougamau-St. Felicien railway line, but it will destroy its effect and the whole area will suffer great wrongs if it puts off that construction. That would work out to the benefit of another area which might be equally concerned but which will gain a foothold, I might say, because we would have to set, to its benefit, a precedent which cannot be but detrimental to the welfare of the Saguenay. We are faced with a problem which can be summarized thus: the railway line, it seems, is to be considered

first from the financial angle. We consider it from that angle but we get the impression that the government will have to plead our case with the C.N.R. which cannot be interested in both sections.
Mr. Speaker, if all that is said and repeated is that we must immediately give a guarantee as to the number of tons that will be shipped, we are placing the district in an unfair position, because if only one section of the railroad is built at a time, it is quite clear that all smelters will be established in the part of the district served by that line and we shall lose them. I wish to mention the possibility of two smelters being built at Chicoutimi and Roberval and that we are jeopardizing those magnificent undertakings, for they will refuse to make risky investments on mere probabilities. They will say that they are willing to build a smelter provided, it goes without saying, they have a railroad. But the government says: "Wait until you build your smelter and then if the development it brings about can ensure sufficient earnings to the railroad, then we will give you that line". Whatever the outcome, we stand to lose.
The member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) certainly echoed the misgivings felt by the people of the Saguenay district, when he requested that both sections be built at the same time. To delay the construction of the Chibougamau-St. Felicien section would be to jeopardize the whole industrial future of the Saguenay district, and, especially, the erection of smelters which can be attracted only by the railway, as well as all other industrial projects awaiting its completion.
In my maiden speech which I delivered in this house on November 24, 1953, I joined the other members from my district in requesting the construction of that section as being essential to the development of my constituency and of this whole area, and I drew the attention of the government, in particular, to the St. Charles iron ore body in my constituency, the richest known so far in titanium content, stating that the development of that ore body was closely associated with this Chibougamau-St. Felicien line, as the traffic on that line would be increased by the construction of smelters.
Power development in my constituency alone exceeds 2,000,000 horsepower per day, as was so eloquently pointed out by the member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon). I am very happy that mention has been made of the millions of cords of pulpwood of which no
Canadian National Railways use could be made failing the immediate construction of that stretch. I feel that the railway should be interested in building this line even if it did not feel that this would bring in immediate revenue, if only because it should have due regard to the evident interest of the Saguenay region and the province as a whole. I really wonder, then, if the Canadian National Railways have done everything possible on the Saguenay side, such as it has done on the other side. We are told, on the authority of the operators concerned with the tonnage which could be transported over t'he Chibougamau-St. Felicien line, that the quantity of lumber in our district is quite sufficient. This is shown by a brief which has just been sent to me by the Saguenay council for economic planning. This quantity would seem to be 75 million feet of lumber, which would be adequate to ensure the railway's revenue. These quantities are confirmed; they would mean close to two million tons transportationwise. That is why I feel somewhat unconvinced of the sincerity of those statements according to which we have no tonnage to transport.
1 believe that, as far as the future is concerned, we have the greatest interest and we have the most numerous outlets, and that is why, in addition to the financial interest, 1 believe that the hon. Minister of Transport must also consider the general interest and the industrial development of a whole area. Therefore I support all those who are asking that both sections of the railway be built at once. Otherwise, it would be unfair and would create a precedent, while jeopardizing the construction of smelters which could only be detrimental to the project already under way in the Saguenay area. A deferred project is always a lost project, and I am under the impression that if the construction of both sections is not ordered immediately, we will be obliged to bring the matter up again, for who can tell that, in 10 or 15 years from now, the financial situation of this country will not be perhaps more difficult for the government, who will then say it is now more difficult and no longer possible to undertake works of that magnitude.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make one or two observations before the debate is closed. I am one of those who believe in the development of our natural resources. In my opinion it is only in the creation of new wealth
4886	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways that we can improve and sustain the standard of living which we enjoy; consequently, it would appear to me to be a good investment on the part of the Canadian people to extend these railroads. No doubt it will help to open up new areas of forests, mines and farms, although I understand the farming areas are more or less limited.
It seems to me that this is a development we can compare with some of the developments that took place in the early days of this country. We would not have made the immense wealth of the west accessible if we had not built the transcontinental railway. This is tapping new areas in the north country that a few years ago we would not have believed it was practical or possible to develop. With the opening up of mining in the north country it looks to me, as I said before, like a good investment.
Along with that, at a time when there is a bit of unemployment-I will minimize it- this will help to create demand for a variety of things which are used in the construction of the railway and of new running gear. All along the line it will be necessary to have maintenance men with homes and families, and consequently businesses will grow up, and villages, towns and probably cities in the not too distant future.
I welcome the legislation, and I hope we go forward with it with all speed. I am convinced that the government is spending many millions of dollars from which they cannot hope to get the return that they will from this investment. I just wish to say that I appreciated the frank and forthright statement made by the minister in his opening remarks when he placed this legislation before us.

subtopic: ST. FELICIEN AND HILLSPORT LINES-PROVISION FOR FINANCING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the minister closes the debate I should like to say a few words on this bill. Several hon. members who spoke in this debate referred to it as a good investment. It would be a very optimistic person indeed who could today with any certainty refer to a railway development, probably in this or in any other country, as a good investment. I agree that this is an essential work for the development of sections of the country that cannot be developed in any other way, and it is interesting to note that it is the Canadian government railway that is building these extensions. I doubt very much whether one could get a private railway company today to invest large sums of money in railway building.
IMr. White (Middlesex East).]

The reason for that is obvious. Today there are other methods of transportation competing, and in my opinion at times unfairly competing, with the railways. Those other methods of transportation are passenger buses, freight-truck lines and air lines, both passenger and freight, and they are taking, as it were, the cream off the transportation business and leaving the unprofitable business to our railways. I have not very much doubt that if something is not done to co-ordinate transportation activity in this country, for years to come, and that not very many years in the future, this government will be paying the deficits on this section of the road, because it requires many different kinds of transportation to make a railway system pay.
To make a railway system pay there has to be considerable express business, as well as considerable passenger traffic, and it is well known that the heavy freight traffic which will inevitably constitute the greatest part of the business of this line will not, at least in my opinion and according to my limited knowledge of transportation, prove a very lucrative business for the railway. However, I agree that this road is necessary for opening up this very difficult section of the country.
In his speech this afternoon the minister mentioned the guarantees on freight obtained by the Canadian National Railways before the project was approved and these guarantees will be all to the good, but they do not cover very many years and it should be kept in mind that when we build a railway it remains in use for a long time in the future. I just wanted to say these things, not because I have any objection to the bill, but because we should go into these matters with our eyes open.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with some of the points brought out during the course of this debate, and more particularly with those which have to do with the reason for beginning the construction of the line in the manner in which the Canadian National Railways has determined.
First of all, however, I should offer an explanation for the question raised by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) and point out that the resolution which was before the house a short time ago referred to the amount of $33,750,000 whereas the bill in one of its sections, I believe section 4, covers an amount of $44,562,500. There is no inconsistency in what is in the resolution, in what is to be found in the schedule to

this bill, and in section 4 of the bill, and I must apologize to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) if I did not follow him carefully, but I think he found the answer.
The answer is to be found in the fact that the amount of $38,750,000 is covered by a 15 per cent estimate, whereby the railways are not authorized to go beyond that amount. In other words, if my hon. friend looks at section 3 of the bill he will find that the company shall not in performing the work of construction and completion exceed such estimates by more than 15 per cent, and the estimates as given in the schedule are for $38,750,000 to which, if 15 per cent is added, one gets the amount of $44,562,500. It is to cover and protect that position that section 4 has been incorporated in the bill.
Now I come to another point, namely that which the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra raised when he said the minister was very uncertain about the construction of this line. He said that he did not know whether the line would begin at the east end or whether it would be continued at the west end, and in fact that there was a great deal of uncertainty. He went on to say the best way to develop industry is to build up the line.
That is the very point that we in this country have been discussing for many years. In years gone by the discussion was as to whether a railway line should be built in order to bring people into the country, or whether the population should first reside in an area before a railway line was built. Evidently it was necessary in earlier years to build the line before the people moved into the area and before industry reached that area if the country was to be developed at all. But we know what the consequences of that policy have been, and during the last few years it has been the policy of this government not to build railway lines, at least through its agency the Canadian National Railways, unless and until there were guarantees which proved that the line could be made profitable.
That was the case in the Kiask-Barraute line; that was the case in the Lynn Lake-Sherridon line, with perhaps a qualification because of the urgent necessity of certain minerals; it was the case in the Kitimat-Terrace line, and it is the case in this line subject to what I will have to say a little later on. Therefore, there is nothing new in the policy which we have been following here, although as I said earlier on the resolution, and as I said on the bill, it may be necessary to give consideration to the payment of a subsidy on this line, dependent upon whether the traffic will or will not develop.
Canadian National Railways
Somewhat to my surprise I found the hon. member raising a question and attempting to prove a point which to my mind is entirely fallacious, namely that the construction of this line will have the effect of diverting Quebec traffic to Toronto. I hope the hon. member will bear with me because from now on I would like to deal with this matter in the French language because the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon), I think the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Girard), and to some extent the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), although he did it in a different manner, repeated this argument.

Canadian National Railways to Beattyville. It is not twice that distance, but only 10 miles longer, or 149 miles. And the editorial adds:

The same applies to the distance by road which is 538 miles from Barraute to Toronto as against only 358 miles from Barraute to Montreal. That is another error in this same article which is aimed at giving the impression that the Canadian National or the federal government would like to direct the traffic movement toward the Abitibi district or rather toward Toronto. The article goes on, in the last paragraph:
These arguments which the premier of the province and the members representing the Lake St. John region put forward are so reasonable that the Canadian government should change its plans in the interests of the Chibougamau district itself and in order to save time and money. The question is of such importance that the interests of Toronto must give precedence to the interests of the entire country.
That argument has been quoted and developed by the hon. member for Chicoutimi. However such an argument proves so very false when analysed that one may wonder why it was even mentioned by him.
Here is why I make such a statement: people who know what all this is about know very well that the copper concentrates from the Chibougamau mines will be sent to Noranda, in the province of Quebec, a fact which was so well stated by the member for Villeneuve (Mr. Dumas) when he asked a question. Moreover, after treatment at Noranda, the copper product will be shipped to a Montreal East refinery, to be further treated in the province of Quebec. From the refinery the material will be shipped for processing in industrial plants again at Montreal, so that every ounce of ore mined in the Chibougamau district will be industrially processed entirely in the province of Quebec and not at Toronto, as the hon. member has wrongly suggested.

speaking of guarantees given to the Canadian National and on which I shall come back a little later, but not of what the hon. member has just mentioned.

Now, I would like to add that, notwithstanding what the hon. members have said, the Canadian National Railways did everything possible to obtain the necessary guarantees from the mining industries and other producers in the eastern part of this district, and, up to now, they have not succeeded in obtaining the necessary guarantees from the financial standpoint.
The question of the transportation of pulp-wood on both sections was raised, and it was stated by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), and the hon. member for Chicoutimi, that those products would be shipped to Toronto. Such an argument is absolutely pointless when we know that in both the province of Quebec and the province of Ontario there are laws providing that pulpwood from either of these two provinces must be processed in the province of origin. It is evident then, in my opinion, that those arguments were brought forth for only one purpose, namely, a political purpose. Some even went further. Some have said: Why is the government's attitude with regard to this line different from the one they adopted with regard to the P.G.E. in British Columbia or the Ontario Northland in Ontario where subsidies were paid? Why should there not be subsidies in a case like this?
Well, here is the answer. It is clear. The government's policy is to encourage lines which can operate at a profit. These two lines were provincial. The first of these two railways belongs to the British Columbia government, and this government wished to extend its trackage. To this end they re-

quested a subsidy, which was granted them. The other line belonged to the province of Ontario. They asked us to subsidize this line years and years ago. That is what he did about that railway, not long ago, and my hon. friend made himself his interpreter, when he said a while ago that the province of Quebec never had the proportion of railways it is entitled to. Another fallacy put forward without any foundation, in an attempt to throw confusion into the minds and to show to certain groups in the province of Quebec that the federal government is not sincere when it tries to build railways to help towards the development of Canada, as is the case at the present time.
I want to develop this argument in order to show that I am right when I say that the province of Quebec has received from the Canadian National, on the basis of its population, as much as the other provinces of our confederation, if not more than any of them.

If my hon. friend will be patient, I think that I can answer the arguments he put forward a while ago. I held my peace when, a moment ago, he made a speech which I did not like; let him listen now to the answers I have for him, because he needs to be answered, for he and others who put forward such arguments are people who want to create disunity in this country, who 83276-310
Canadian National Railways do not want a Canadian confederation, but who claim for Quebec a situation apart, different from that of the other provinces.
Here is the situation, Mr. Speaker. In the province of Saskatchewan, for instance, there are 8,739 miles of single-track railroad lines and that is the province with the longest system even if its population cannot be compared to that of the province of Quebec. In fact, in the case of Saskatchewan, there are 10-5 miles of railroad per thousand people. Because in a province the ratio of population per mile of railroad is higher, because that province is at the same time the second in area-let us say per mile of railroad track- it must not be inferred that that province is deficient in railroad facilities. In the province of Quebec there is a concentration of population around Montreal but there are very few inhabitants in Ungava, in Abitibi, in various parts of Labrador and of Baffin Land. These boundless regions are practically uninhabited. One must not conclude that the railroad facilities are lacking in that province. It does not mean that railroad facilities are inferior in comparison to its population, for they are equal if not superior to the facilities in some provinces.
In fact, the economic vitality of Montreal does not depend as much on the province as on the whole of Canada. When that factor is taken into account, we find that the number of inhabitants per mile of railroad is in agreement with the average for Canada. Industry in the province has not been handicapped in the least and the necessary facilities have been provided without delay and as soon as they were requested.
Has the province of Quebec been neglected? I hear people say, even in this house, that the province of Quebec has been neglected by the Canadian National. Let us examine what has been done by the Canadian National by way of expenditures in the province of Quebec, under the present government. During the past five years the Canadian National Railways have spent large sums to improve and expand facilities in the province of Quebec. For instance, they spent $25,740,000 in 1949; $23,906,000 in 1950; $24,412,000 in 1951; $26,805,000 in 1952, or a total of $100,863,000 in less than four years, and I do not take into account 1953 and the first part of 1954. If all those figures were added, the total would be in the neighbourhood of $150,000,000.
