Besides, the Canadian National Railways from 1948 to 1952 paid out $319 million in salaries in the province of Quebec alone. Moreover, a substantial portion of the money spent by the Canadian National Railways for the extension of the operation department- diesel engines-and rolling stock went to the province of Quebec. These expenses, for the years 1948-52, are as follows:	1948,
$14,962,000; 1949, $5,265,000; 1950, $22,600,000; 1951, $24,431,000; 1952, $36,892,000; that is $103,650,000 in all.
My hon. friend interrupted me a while ago to tell me that the Chicoutimi district had not been developed. But such was not his argument when he made his plea. His argument was that the province of Quebec had been neglected and now he is suggesting we have neglected the Chicoutimi district. The Chicoutimi district is not neglected since we are asking the house for permission to begin a railway in those parts; yet you complain claiming we are not starting construction at the right end. I will tell you why we are not starting at your end. If you find I am speaking too sharply, you have no one to blame but yourselves.
We are starting with the Beattyville-Chibougamau stretch because we have traffic guarantees which show that the Canadian National Railways will be assured of a profit of $23,000 a year. But do you know what the financial position of the railway would be if we were to begin at the other end? It would mean a deficit of at least one million dollars a year. There is the answer. That is why the Canadian National Railways has recommended to the government that construction be started from the west rather than from the east. But the government wanted parliament to authorize the building of that line, of the whole line in the interest of the Saguenay district and also in the interest of the Chicoutimi area. In other words, we are asking for a charter, so that the line may be completely built, and we hope that, during the period of construction, a zinc refinery may be established at Chicoutimi, and that other industrial developments may take place, which will make the extension of this line possible. However, the reason for which we are beginning with the western section is found in the financial aspect; that is the only reason, for let us remember that there are other parts of Canada where railways should be built; there are other parts of Canada that have been asking for many years that such railroads be [Mr. Chevrler.l

built, and we also often have had the Canadian National make a survey of such proposed roads. The Canadian National found that they should not be built, because its financial position would not be improved by their construction. Why should another policy be followed with regard to the Chibougamau line? One part would be profitable, while the other would not.
We are starting with the profitable end and will continue with the other as soon as we can get guarantees.
My hon. friend is very much interested in the development of his own district; may I tell him this: it will cost $17 million to build the eastern section, that is the section from St. Felicien to Chibougamau.
Now, if the government of the province of Quebec wants to pay half these building costs, namely 8 million and a half, I undertake to ask the Canadian National to spend the other half, namely 8 million and a half. Then we shall see who is sincere.
For the government, Mr. Speaker, this is not a matter of politics; it is an economic matter and nothing else.
I should rather address my remarks to the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), who has unfortunately made a purely political speech this afternoon.
I have respect for the hon. member, but not for the speech he made this afternoon. At least it can be said that the members who are seated at the end of this house have studied the matter and know what they are talking about. Department of Transport Act to the Emergency Powers Act, to make certain regulations with reference to transport control. Mr. Speaker, from my reading of the bill, and from listening to the explanation given by the minister, this group has no objection to passing it. I think the principle of putting in statute form what the government can do, rather than to have it done by order in council as was done under the Emergency Powers Act, is something for which we have been asking on this side of the house for some time. The legislation may not have been used, and we have no reason to suppose that it will be used in the future any more than it has been in the past unless an emergency does arise.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) mentioned the one case where the controller did use these
Department of Transport Act powers to give priority of grain over iron ore where it was necessary to move grain quickly. Somebody should have that power so that the country may receive transportation, not according to the wishes of a few individuals but according to the wishes of those who are administering in the interests' of the economy as a whole. I do not see that we have any objection at all to the passage of this bill.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
On clause 1-Control of transport of goods in bulk.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: My understanding is that the controller has operated successfully and satisfactorily to those concerned. Like the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, I am puzzled as to the need for this wide extension. Perhaps the minister can tell us a little as to the way it has been operated. For example, I should like to know the staff the controller has. What has been the scope and what has he controlled so far? Then I should like some further explanation as to the extremely wide range that is now proposed. Let me reiterate, my understanding is that it has worked well to date.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext:
It has worked very well to date. In so far as the difference in the powers is concerned, there is some difference, as pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre himself. He read the preamble to the order in council, which refers to the international emergency, security, defence, peace, order and good government and the like. These powers are not referred to in the bill. The only reference in the bill is that it is necessary to take these powers in order to meet export commitments and domestic needs. But the position has been such that the transport controller and the method under which he has operated have been so successful that these powers should be continued. They should be continued, too, because the fact that he has operated in the past in the manner in which he has indicates that there has been no tie-up in the movement of those grains and other commodities. He has attempted not to use the powers arbitrarily. I do not think it can be said that he has, and I doubt whether he has issued many orders. Certainly, he has not issued many, but what he has been able to do on a number of occasions is to indicate to shipping companies and the like the fact that he had the powers, and to suggest to them that they should move the commodities in a certain fashion. That has been extremely successful and might be required

Department of Transport Act at any moment. So far as the staff is concerned, it is very small. There are only six.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: That is the l-eason I am asking the question. I wanted that brought out. Apparently up to date he has operated with a small staff. Therefore I take it he has not found it necessary to interfere very much with operations.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: I can appreciate that this government has got itself so involved in the grain business that it is necessary to control the shipment and storage of grain. But is there any such shortage of shipping or transportation that we need a controller to handle products like ferrous metals, iron and steel scrap, pulpwood, sand, stone and gravel, and so on? Has any control of that kind been exercised? If not, what is the apprehension at this time which makes it necessary to have a controller of such a wide range of .commodities which have been moving freely?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: May I say a word *on that subject? All those commodities are of the kind that move in bulk, and they use the same type of equipment, whether rail equipment or boat equipment. Frequently a suggestion has gone out that certain boats be diverted from ore to wheat. The reason for that is that there is an urgent demand for certain grades of wheat, and the demand for ore is not urgent. I may say that the transport controller is one of the busiest officials of the government. He works closely with my department through the interest of trade and commerce in the movement of wheat. The fact that he does not issue written orders under a statute is solely for the reason that all forms of transportation recognize the benefit to them of having someone direct their operations in a way that will cause them the minimum of delay and will give them loads. When they arrive at a port there will be a load waiting for them. He generally looks at the over-all transportation system to use the available equipment to the best advantage. It is one of the most successful operations. We are fortunate in having a very able controller, a man who thoroughly understands his business and the problems involved. If you were to ask any of the transportation companies whether they would desire to have a controller with the powers indicated in this bill you would have the unanimous opinion that that was their desire.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: Oh, no. Two years ago there was an acute shortage of lake shipping. It is true that additional lake carriers have been built since then, but it was a very close decision as to which was more urgent, the movement of wheat, the movement of iron ore or the movement of pulpwood from down river in the St. Lawrence. That was under constant study by the transport controller, and boats were used in a way that every necessary movement was taken care of. In that year we were not able to move all the wheat we would have liked to move. We were not able to move all the iron ore we would have liked to move, but the essentials of all trade were moved due to the very careful study and arrangements by the transport controller.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: The minister agrees that this is still an emergency measure?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: Perhaps not an emergency, but we have a very serious congestion already. I just left a committee that was studying the problem of a car cycle of moving wheat from country elevators in a way that would be fair to the various interests involved, and that would get a fair distribution of transportation as far as the distributors are concerned. I am sure that the transport controller will be able to solve that problem. He is a very essential official, in my opinion, as far as the movement of wheat is concerned, and no one can concentrate on wheat without having regard to other bulk commodities which must move at-the same time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the other day I asked the minister about the control of ships and in particular whether there was any control over Japanese ships, and he said I should wait until the bill was introduced because the word "ship" would be defined in the bill. But I cannot find any definition in the bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext:
What I had in mind was
that it was defined in the regulations, wherein a ship was defined as a ship of 1,000 gross registered tons or over, or designated as being capable of being so used, and I have presumed that when we pass an order in council under this legislation we will use the same definition.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: Is it the intention that the bill apply only to great lakes ships, or will it apply to deep-sea vessels on the coastal trade?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: It is the intention to apply it to all ships of 1,000 gross registered tons operating in Canadian waters.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: Why is it necessary to apply this to coastal ships? As I understand it the whole problem surely revolves around the wheat trade and the only place in which ships have to be controlled is in the great lakes. Now why not restrict the control accordingly, rather than have this over-all control?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext:
That is a matter I think
which should be discussed with the transport controller.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext:
Two or three years ago we had a very serious problem in moving coal from Sydney into the St. Lawrence ports and the transport controller had to allocate ships to undertake that movement. Any bulk movement taking place in Canadian waters should I think be properly
Department of Transport Act subjected to the jurisdiction of the transport controller. If you do not want him to exercise control on the Pacific coast then I have no objection to striking it out. It is of no interest to me, but I think the shipping companies would be happier if they were able to call upon the transport controller when necessary.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: There is one feature in this bill which I think requires further consideration. The Minister of Transport has rather intimated that this is an emergency measure, and now the Minister of Trade and Commerce has intimated that he thinks it might be a good thing to carry this right through, and the bill itself is only for a period of two years.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: We think it will be a good thing for that period.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: Is it the government's intention that this will be a permanent form of control, or is it to be merely temporary?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: That is a matter which will be decided two years hence.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: The bill covers storage, but I do not see how the dominion government obtained the power to control storage under the British North America Act. I can understand them having the power under the Emergency Powers Act, and I can see where they might control transportation by ordinary legislation, but how does the government get control over storage?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: On grain.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: That cannot be the basis for legislation. Surely the control of storage comes under the provincial government.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: Not in the grain trade.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: But this bill applies not only to grain but to many other commodities such as sand, stone, gravel, logs, coal and coke. Could the Minister of Transport tell us how the dominion government obtained jurisdiction to legislate on the storage of commodities of that kind?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext:
It certainly has jurisdiction over storage facilities which belong to the federal government such as elevators, wharves, piers on which are built transit sheds. The ships that operate from such points and which have not been covered thus far are ships which carry commodities from these points. My hon. friend may have raised a legal point of some significance but all I can say is that this bill was subjected to very careful study by the committee presided over by the Minister of Justice, and

Department of Transport Act I am sure the bill was examined from that angle. But all I can say on the point raised is that the facilities now used are facilities over which we have jurisdiction.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, let me point out that the minister has not given a categorical answer to this question. We have had 25 minutes, if my reckoning is correct, to consider this important measure, and it seems to me that the matter is not quite so vital that we should rush it through now and find out afterwards that something was overlooked. It is conceivable that the justice department overlooked that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: On that question of storage, if the suggestion is that storage was used which was not under government control then the transport controller could not attempt to exercise control and his jurisdiction could be challenged. Practically all bulk commodities use government facilities for storage, though grain is stored under public authority. The use of storage is a matter which the transport controller has to decide. He might perhaps allow American grain to be shipped through a Canadian elevator under the jurisdiction of the board of grain commissioners. But that question is for him to decide and he must decide whether the storage space is more urgently needed for Canadian grain.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: Would it be possible to cut down some of these articles listed under section 2?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: If it is possible why is it necessary?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: Simply for the reason that I do not think the dominion government has very much business attempting to take over the control of the storage of such things as coal, logs, sand, stone and gravel. I think this is a case of taking over wider powers than are required. The main objective, of course, is to control the grain and to that there is no objection, but I suggest that consideration be given to narrowing down the list of goods which come under control. I think control is largely a matter of suggestion. I know the transport controller simply suggests that such and such a thing be done, but in so far as government facilities are concerned, or government wheat, any government official designated could control them. Such an official would not necessarily have to have transport control. However, is it not possible to cut down the number of commodities which are to be made subject to control?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext:
It is possible to do without the bill altogether, and it is possible to put in wheat and nothing else.


If my hon. friend wants to make a motion that anything be struck out, and if that motion carries the approval of the committee, I will not object as long as he leaves wheat and iron ore in it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am wondering whether it would be possible to have control of one commodity. Is it not a fact that if the controller is going to issue an order for the transportation of wheat or of grain, then the other commodities that are being transported at that time have to give way to the transport of wheat? It seems to me that it is quite impossible to have it apply to grain only, although the minister said he was quite willing that it should. I do not think his judgment in this case is as good as it usually is. I think it would be quite impossible to have it refer to only one item such as grain. If there are plenty of ships to take care of all the grain, then no order need be issued. But if ships are being used for the other commodities mentioned in this bill and if those ships are wanted for grain, I think those other commodities will have to give way and give priority to grain. That is the whole purpose of the bill, so far as I can see.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if I may, I should just like to clear up that point. I say that the bill, as it is, is a desirable bill. My sole interest in the transport controller happens to be in connection with the movement of wheat. I therefore say that I would not object if the committee wants to cut out other items. However, I am sure other people would object.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: The minister's interests are not so narrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: As I say, I do not know of any other government officer whose work has been as well received by everyone as has the work of the transport controller. He knows his job. He has taken care of every commodity that needed to be moved. If someone wants to move rock salt-and there is quite a bit of that commodity moved -he provides boats for the movement of it. If someone needs to move coal from Cape Breton island up the St. Lawrence, he finds boats for that movement. He uses his best judgment to divide the boats between the movement of wheat and the movement of iron ore and to see that they are moved at the proper season. There has been some question about it but in the end everybody has been satisfied. I think it is a perfect bill as it stands. It simply provides for carrying out the duties that have been imposed upon him for several years. I think the bill should pass.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL OF GOODS IN BULK
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I was going to express some of the ideas the minister has advanced. Hon. members on this side of the house are glad to And reasons to criticize the government, but I do not think any member of any party has been critical of the outstanding job the controller has done. When the problem at Rama was brought to the controller's attention, namely that Rama farmers had not been able to deliver the five-bushel quota, action was taken immediately and additional cars were sent there. If this grain is going to be moved to the overseas market when ships are available he has to have authority to hold up the movement of pulp or gravel or some of the other things if the wheat is to move. I think the fact that opposition members have not had many critical remarks to make with regard to the work of the transport controller would indicate that it would be an extremely unpopular move if this legislation should be killed.
